newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols deflate as dollar bounces.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols deflate as dollar bounces.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options, particularly the short dates, deflated almost as quickly as they swelled earlier in the week after the dollar's sharp reversal rally overnight, dealers said.

"I'm not sure if it's warranted, but that's what the market is doing," a U.S. bank trader in Chicago said of the acute recoil in the implieds. "We're back in the previous range here, but it all occurred in a few days and there could be some follow-throughs."
The dollar, which had touched a seven-month low of 110.62 yen on Wednesday, rallied toward 115.70 overnight.
It has since been circling the 114-yen area through most of European and U.S. trading.

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen options stood at around 12.3/12.5 percent in early U.S. afternoon, down about 2.5 point from late Wednesday levels. One-year was also off a full point to 10.5/10.7 percent.

Risk reversals, the put/call pricing differential, narrowed their extremely strong skew for yen calls as fears of a further dollar dive below 110 yen subsided. One-month 25-delta, which on Wednesday had gone up to 2.5 point in favor of yen calls, shrank to about 1.5/2.0.
The dollar's rebound was triggered by remarks by an influential Japanese finance ministry official that rises in Japan's trade surplus were being played up too much.
"I think there's a good chance, with the sharp upmove in dollar/yen, that we have put in a bottom," said a U.S. bank trader in California. "It's met a lot of people's objectives."
But she noted that potential for wild spot movements and nervousness had yet to go away and that the shorter-dated options continued to be valued above the longer-maturities.
"To sell volatility (outright), I'd like to see the market calm down a bit," she said.
She said selling risk-reversals -- selling the richly priced downside yen calls and buying yen puts -- was starting to look attractive to delta-neutral volatility traders.

Through such a trade, a trader can take in some premium without changing the overall volatility position very much. However, gamma exposure on the short side could be very painful should the dollar threaten the downside again.

In fact, traders said risk-reversal buying in recent days, more likely to have been of protective nature than speculation because they would have incurred large premium payment, has backfired as the dollar bounced sharply today.
"Anybody who sold puts (near spot's lows), it worked well from a volatility standpoint but from a gamma standpoint it wasn't the thing to do," the Chicago trader said.
Dollar/mark volatilities were slightly softer as the dollar edged higher within recent 1.69-1.74 mark ranges.

"It doesn't seem to matter how big the intraday move is if the direction is toward an old range," the Chicago trader said. The dollar tested 1.73 marks in the U.S. after trading mostly below 1.72 in the past few days.
One-month dollar/mark stood at 9.2/9.4 percent, off about 0.2 point. One-year was little changed at 9.4/9.6.
